```{r setup}
library(adorn)
add_one <- function(x) x + 1
```

`vignette("writing-decorators")` shows decorators that work. This vignette is
about writing ones that keep working: how to choose between the two styles,
what a decorated call costs, and the mistakes that are easy to make. Every
example below is run when the vignette is built, so the output shown is what you
will see.

## Choosing a style

`decorator()` looks at the signature of the function you give it.

| | Call style | Factory style |
|---|---|---|
| Signature | `function(f, ..., options)` | `function(f, options)` |
| The body runs | on **every call** of the decorated function | **once**, when the function is decorated |
| It returns | the result of the call | a function that replaces `f` |
| State | none; locals are new each call | one set per decorated function |
| Good for | logging, timing, argument checks, retries | caching, counters, run-once, setup work |

The rule of thumb is that if the decorator needs to remember anything between
calls, or has setup work that does not depend on the arguments, it is a
factory. Otherwise a call-style decorator is shorter.

## What a decorated call costs

adorn adds roughly a microsecond to each call, and about the same again for
each decorator you stack. A plain function call takes about a tenth of that. The
exact numbers depend on your machine, so measure your own.

```r
null_dec <- decorator(function(f, ...) f(...))
fast <- function(x) x + 1
decorated <- null_dec %@% fast

bench::mark(raw = fast(5), decorated = decorated(5))
```

For a function that does real work, such as reading a file, calling an API or
fitting a model, that overhead is not measurable. It only matters for functions
that finish in a few microseconds *and* are called millions of times. In that
case, the cost of your own wrapper code will usually dominate what adorn adds,
and that is the part you control.

## Pitfalls

### State in a call-style decorator

A call-style body runs again on every call, so anything it creates is thrown
away. This counter never gets past 1:

```{r state-bad}
counter_bad <- decorator(function(f, ...) {
  n <- 0
  n <- n + 1
  cat("call", n, "\n")
  f(...)
})

bad <- counter_bad %@% add_one
invisible(bad(1))
invisible(bad(1))
```

Make it a factory. The body now runs once per decorated function, and the
function it returns closes over `n`. Each decorated function gets its own copy:

```{r state-good}
counter <- decorator(function(f) {
  n <- 0
  function(...) {
    n <<- n + 1
    cat("call", n, "\n")
    f(...)
  }
})

first <- counter %@% add_one
second <- counter %@% add_one
invisible(first(1))
invisible(first(1))
invisible(second(1))
```

### Work done on every call that could be done once

In a call-style decorator, anything before `f(...)` runs on every call. If it
does not depend on the arguments, move it into a factory. `memoize` in
`vignette("writing-decorators")` does this: it hashes the function once, then
each call only hashes its arguments.

The same applies to `decorator_context()`. It looks at the call stack, which is
much more expensive than the rest of a decorator, and the cost grows with each
stacked decorator, because each level looks outward through the levels above it.
Asking for the context on every call, in four stacked decorators, costs several
times as much as the decorators themselves:

```r
per_call <- decorator(function(f, ...) {
  name <- decorator_context()$name
  f(...)
})
once <- decorator(function(f) {
  name <- decorator_context()$name
  function(...) f(...)
})

lvl4_per_call <- per_call %@% per_call %@% per_call %@% per_call %@% add_one
lvl4_once <- once %@% once %@% once %@% once %@% add_one

bench::mark(per_call = lvl4_per_call(5), once = lvl4_once(5), check = FALSE)
```

On the machine this was written on, that was about 35µs per call against about
5µs. Both are fast in absolute terms, so this only matters in a hot loop.

The two do not return the same name, so which one you want depends on what the
name is for. In a factory, `decorator_context()` runs while the function is
being decorated, before any call exists, so the name is the one the function was
bound to at that point. In a call-style decorator it is the name the function
was *called* by:

```{r context-names}
at_setup <- decorator(function(f) {
  cat("setup sees:", decorator_context()$name, "\n")
  function(...) f(...)
})
at_call <- decorator(function(f, ...) {
  cat("call sees: ", decorator_context()$name, "\n")
  f(...)
})

fn_a <- at_setup %@% add_one
fn_b <- at_call %@% add_one

invisible(fn_b(1))
alias <- fn_b
invisible(alias(1))
invisible(lapply(1, fn_b))
```

The last line shows the fallback. When there is no usable name in the call, as
with `FUN` inside `lapply()`, you get the name the function was decorated under.
If you want a name that follows each call, such as for logging, use call style
and accept the cost. If you just want a label that identifies the function, ask
once in a factory.

#### Anonymous functions

A function with no name has nothing to report at setup. `%@%` only sees the
function, not the variable you assign the result to, so a factory that reads the
name while it is being decorated gets `"<anonymous>"`:

```{r anonymous-setup}
setup_name <- decorator(function(f) {
  name <- decorator_context()$name
  function(...) {
    cat("->", name, "\n")
    f(...)
  }
})

anon <- setup_name %@% function(x) x + 1
invisible(anon(1))
```

The name exists once the function is called, so ask for it on the first call
and keep it. This costs one stack lookup, once, and nothing after that:

```{r anonymous-lazy}
traced <- decorator(function(f) {
  name <- NULL
  function(...) {
    if (is.null(name)) {
      name <<- decorator_context()$name
    }
    cat("->", name, "\n")
    f(...)
  }
})

plus_one <- traced %@% function(x) x + 1
invisible(plus_one(1))
```

This has two limits. The first call decides the name, so if the function is later
called through an alias, it keeps the original name. And a call that carries no
name, such as `FUN` inside `lapply()`, or `do.call()` with the function itself,
gives `"<anonymous>"`. If that is the first call, it is the name you keep:

```{r anonymous-weakness}
fn <- traced %@% function(x) x
invisible(lapply(1, fn))
invisible(fn(1))
```

If you need the right name in those cases, call `decorator_context()` on every
call, as in call style, and accept the cost.

If you can name the function when you decorate it, the problem goes away. `%@%`
takes a `name` argument, so the name is known at setup:

```{r anonymous-name}
setup_name_again <- decorator(function(f) {
  name <- decorator_context()$name
  function(...) {
    cat("->", name, "\n")
    f(...)
  }
})

add_three <- `%@%`(setup_name_again, function(x) x + 3, name = "add_three")
invisible(add_three(1))
invisible(lapply(1, add_three))
```

The development version of S7 has a `:=` operator that fills `name` in from the
left-hand side, so you do not have to write it out.

```{r anonymous-walrus, eval = FALSE}
library(S7)

add_two := setup_name_again %@% function(x) x + 2
invisible(add_two(1))
#> -> add_two
invisible(lapply(1, add_two))
#> -> add_two
```

`:=` only works with a plain variable on the left, so it does not help for
`obj$method := ...`; pass `name` directly there.

`decorator_context()` only works inside a decorator and gives an error anywhere
else:

```{r context-outside, error = TRUE}
decorator_context()
```

### Losing `invisible()`

Functions that return `invisible()` stay quiet when a call-style decorator
returns `f(...)` directly. Assigning the result first loses that, and the value
prints:

```{r visible}
quiet <- function() invisible("done")

forwards <- decorator(function(f, ...) f(...))
assigns <- decorator(function(f, ...) {
  result <- f(...)
  result
})

(forwards %@% quiet)()
(assigns %@% quiet)()
```

If the decorator has to do something after the call and still return the result,
`withVisible()` keeps the visibility:

```{r withvisible}
keeps <- decorator(function(f, ...) {
  result <- withVisible(f(...))
  # ... work after the call goes here ...
  if (result$visible) result$value else invisible(result$value)
})

(keeps %@% quiet)()
```

### Recursion goes through the decorator every time

A decorated function that calls itself calls the decorated version, so the
decorator runs on every level of the recursion. That is what you want for
`memoize`, and not what you want for a decorator that does something visible,
such as timing:

```{r recursion}
n_calls <- 0
count <- decorator(function(f, ...) {
  n_calls <<- n_calls + 1
  f(...)
})

fib <- count %@% function(n) if (n < 2) n else fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)
fib(5)
n_calls
```

One call to `fib(5)` ran the decorator 15 times. If you only want the outermost
call, decorate a small wrapper that calls an undecorated recursive function
instead.

### Order of stacked decorators

In `a %@% b %@% f`, `a` is the outermost decorator. Its code before `f(...)`
runs first, and its code after runs last:

```{r order}
a <- decorator(function(f, ...) {
  cat("a in\n")
  result <- f(...)
  cat("a out\n")
  result
})
b <- decorator(function(f, ...) {
  cat("b in\n")
  result <- f(...)
  cat("b out\n")
  result
})

(a %@% b %@% add_one)(1)
```

When the order matters, such as `retry` inside `timed` against `timed` inside
`retry`, the first measures all the attempts and the second measures each one.

### Reading errors

An error raised in a decorator's *own* code is reported against the decorator,
with the call `name(f, ...)`. An error from the decorated function keeps its own
call:

```{r errors, error = TRUE}
bad_dec <- decorator(function(f, ...) {
  stop("oops")
  f(...)
})
plain <- decorator(function(f, ...) f(...))

(bad_dec %@% add_one)(1)
(plain %@% function(x) stop("inner"))(1)
```

The name comes from the variable the decorator was assigned to, so `bad_dec`
shows as `bad_dec`. If you write a decorator inline and want a stable name in
errors and in `decorators()`, pass `name =` to `decorator()`.

### Mistakes `decorator()` catches for you

`decorator()` checks the signature when you define it, and a factory is checked
when it is applied:

```{r signature, error = TRUE}
# The function to decorate must be the first argument.
decorator(function(...) 1)

# In call style, `...` must come straight after it.
decorator(function(f, x, ...) 1)

# A factory must return a function.
not_a_function <- decorator(function(f) 1)
not_a_function %@% add_one
```

## A checklist

Before you publish a decorator:

- Does it need to remember something between calls? Use a factory.
- Is there setup work that does not depend on the arguments? Do it in the
  factory, not on every call.
- Does it return `f(...)` directly, or use `withVisible()`, so `invisible()`
  results stay invisible?
- Does it call `decorator_context()` per call? If you only need a label, call it
  once in a factory, and for anonymous functions on the first call.
- Would recursion or stacking change what it does?
- Does it have a `name`, so errors and `decorators()` read well?
